claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is an example of a single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy is a disordered solid solution with negligible SRO at high temperatures.
Intermediate-temperature isothermal annealing can evolve SRO from isolated clusters into a percolating network while retaining the single-phase bcc structure.
The proposed annealing regime is below the solvus but above the ordering temperature.
The proposed operating range is 0.4 Tm to 0.7 Tm at 1 atm.
Quenching to room temperature preserves the high-temperature SRO configuration.
SRO clusters undergo a percolative transition upon reaching a critical volume fraction and spatial connectivity.
A percolating SRO network creates low-thermal-conductivity pathways.
The percolative SRO transition causes a nonlinear, super-additive reduction in lattice thermal conductivity beyond standard scattering-model predictions.
Chemically ordered domains disrupt phonon mean free paths through coherent-interface scattering and mass-difference fluctuations.
Connected SRO regions possess a vibrational density of states distinct from that of the disordered matrix.
The connected SRO network acts as a percolative barrier to phonon transport.
Effective thermal conductivity drops precipitously when the SRO connectivity threshold is crossed.
After the threshold-associated drop, lattice thermal conductivity plateaus or declines more slowly.
The threshold-associated conductivity change cannot be explained by summing individual-cluster scattering cross-sections.
Debye-Callaway or serial/parallel effective-medium baselines predict a linear or sub-linear decrease in lattice thermal conductivity with increasing SRO concentration.
The hypothesized behavior requires SRO-induced local-force-constant changes without transformation to an ordered intermetallic or a non-bcc structure.
The percolation threshold depends on pair-interaction energies and SRO-evolution kinetics.
Anharmonic effects may influence the measured conductivity drop and may be difficult to separate from percolative scattering.
Coincidence between a structurally identified connectivity threshold and a sharp conductivity drop would distinguish the proposed transition from a linear dilute-scattering response.
